Justices Grant Republican Emergency Appeal on Midterm TV Ad Rates
                     
                
                WASHINGTON — The Supreme Court on Friday granted an emergency request from Republican campaign committees to temporarily block a lower-court ruling that had restricted their access to preferential broadcast advertising rates.
The unsigned order will enable the National Republican Congressional Committee and the National Republican Senatorial Committee to purchase airtime at lower costs reserved for candidates as they head into the 2026 midterm elections.
It overturns a decision by the 4th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals, which had previously sided with Democratic candidates challenging the Federal Communications Commission’s interpretation of federal campaign finance rules.
The 4th Circuit had held that the preferential rates, which are significantly lower than standard commercial rates, were intended exclusively for individual candidates for personal use, rather than party-coordinated advertising.
The Republican committees had petitioned the high court to intervene, arguing that the appeals court’s decision created immediate operational confusion for broadcasters and disrupted campaign budget planning with the general election approaching.
They contended that the 4th Circuit acted prematurely, as the FCC had not yet issued a final order on the matter.
U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer filed a brief supporting the Republican request. In his filing, Sauer argued that the challengers lacked the legal standing to sue because the FCC’s original guidance offered the same benefits to all parties involved, including the Democratic challengers.
The dispute centers on a March 30, 2026, public notice issued by the FCC’s Media Bureau, which indicated that political parties and joint fundraising committees could access the same discounted rates as candidates during the 45-day window before a primary and the 60-day window before a general election.
Democratic candidates, including Sen. Jon Ossoff of Georgia, challenged the notice in federal court, arguing that it violated the intent of federal election law. They asserted that the rule provided an unfair financial advantage to Republican committees, which generally possess larger fundraising caches than individual Democratic candidates.
As is their custom, the justices in the majority did not provide a detailed explanation for the ruling.
In the lone dissent, Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson said she believes the Republicans won’t ultimately succeed on the merits of their argument that the 4th Circuit lacked statutory jurisdiction in this case.
Friday’s action keeps the appeals court ruling on hold while the legal challenge proceeds.
Broadcasters and campaigns are expected to operate under the FCC’s original guidance regarding ad rates until the Supreme Court provides further instruction or the case is resolved through the standard appellate process.

Written by LINDSAY WHITEHURST Associated Press
The Supreme Court granted an emergency appeal from Republicans in a dispute over campaign ad prices on Friday, clearing a legal roadblock to political parties getting cheaper TV ad time ahead of the midterm elections.
The justices halted for now a lower-court ruling in favor of Democratic candidates who argued that cheaper broadcast ads should be limited to candidates. One justice publicly dissented from the unsigned order. It’s the latest election-related appeal to come before the high court ahead of the pivotal November contests.
The Trump administration supported the emergency appeal from GOP campaign arms.
The decision comes on the heels of a June Supreme Court ruling that removed limits on parties spending money in coordination with candidates. It was seen as a boon to the GOP because the national party has a sizable cash advantage, and access to cheaper ad rates could boost that edge.
Among Democrats, meanwhile, some individual candidates have sizable fundraising advantages over their Republican opponents.
Candidates pay discounted rates for TV time around an election under federal law, and in March the Federal Communications Commission’s Media Bureau said certain party-coordinated ads are entitled to those prices as well.
Four Democrats, including Sen. Jon Ossoff of Georgia and former Sen. Sherrod Brown of Ohio, challenged the finding in court. They won a victory from a divided panel of the U.S. 4th Circuit Court of appeals.
The National Republican Congressional Committee and National Republican Senatorial Committee then asked the Supreme Court to intervene. They argued that broadcasters were already charging them higher rates and upending their planned budgets after the appeals court decision.
The majority of justices agreed that the lower court had acted too soon with the order that differed from judges around the country.
“Current and future recissions will require the party committees to pay more for advertising space, thereby hampering their efforts to reach the electorate in the critical weeks leading up to the midterms,” the Supreme Court order states.
One justice, Ketanji Brown Jackson, disagreed, writing that the court likely didn’t have to wait until an internal FCC review was done.
The decision halts the appeals court ruling while the Republican committees file a fuller appeal.
